list.listitem: Use validated clinical decision rules such as the POUND criteria, ICHD diagnostic criteria and Three-item Migraine Screener to differentiate the three main primary headaches.B Use SNNOOP10 mnemonic for secondary causes of headache, and use The Ottawa Subarachnoid Hemorrhage Rule to help identify subarachnoid hemorrage.
Image all patients with focal neurological deficits.B

Strongly consider imaging and/or additional specific testing such as lumbar puncture for patients with a red flag for serious disease (eg, thunderclap headache, new-onset headache after age 50 years, malignancy or HIV disease, seizures, or headache precipitated by Valsalva).B
The absence of red flags may suggest that no work up is needed.

Headache is defined by the International Headache Society (IHS) as "pain located in the head, above the orbitomeatal line and/or nuchal ridge." The International Classification of Headache Disorder, 3rd edition has significantly improved the categorization of headaches.

A primary headache has no known underlying cause. Secondary headache is the result of another condition causing traction on or inflammation of pain-sensitive structures. Secondary headache "may have the characteristics of a primary headache but still fulfill criteria for causation by another disorder". Headache due to psychiatric disease or headache attributed to a substance or its withdrawal, is also considered secondary.
Considerations for primary headaches include migraine, tension-type headache, trigeminal autonomic cephalagias and other primary headache disorders.

Headaches related to trauma, vascular disorder, non-vascular intracranial disorder, infection, substance abuse, substance withdrawal, medication overuse, and psychiatric disorders are examples of more common secondary headaches.

Migraine is a common, multifactorial, disabling, recurrent, hereditary neurovascular headache disorder. Collectively, the symptoms that accompany migraine from the prodoromal stage through the headache phase suggest that multiple neuronal systems function abnormally.

Tension-type headache is a dull, bilateral, mild-to-moderate intensity pressure type pain without striking associated features that may be categorized as infrequent, frequent, or chronic and is easily distinguished from migraine. Tenderness of pericranial muscles, co-existing mood disorders, and mechanical disorders of the spine and neck may be contributing factors.

Trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias (TACs) are a group of primary headaches disorders characterized by short-lasting episodes of severe unilateral headaches that are associated with ipsilateral cranial autonomic symptoms and include cluster headache (CH), paroxysmal hemicranias (PH) and short-lasting unilateral neuralgiform headache with conjunctival injection and tearing (SUNCT)/shortlasting unilateral neuralgiform headache attacks with cranial autonomic features (SUNA).
See for the incidence of primary headaches in different age groups worldwide.
The incidence of headache from secondary pathology in the United States is brain tumors 4.6/1000, subarachnoid hemorrhage 0.9/1000.
Headache is more common in Europe and North America than in Asia or South America (for example, 80% in a Canadian survey).
Lifelong prevalence of headache is 96%, with a female predominance. The global active prevalence of tension-type headache is approximately 40% and migraine 10% -14.7%.
A total of 1.2 million patients present to US emergency departments annually with migraine headache.

Migraine is now ranked by the World Health Organization as number 19 among all diseases worldwide causing disability. According to the 2016 Global Burden of Disease Study, migraine is the second leading cause of Years Lived with Disability, and ranks 16th on Disability Adjusted Life Years, which measures health loss due to both fatal and non-fatal disease burden.
Prevalence of migraine: 15% to 18% of women, 6% of men.
If women only taken into consideration, migraine ranks 12th in terms of disability induced by various disorders.
Migraine occurs most commonly in men and women aged 25 to 55 years.
Neurologists worldwide estimate that 18% of patients with a headache have a secondary headache disorder.
The prevalence of medication overuse headache among the adult population is 0.5% to 7.2% and is the most common secondary headache disroder.

Primary headaches entail a variety of negative repercussions, both on individuals and on society at large. They result in heavy financial costs, either direct (expenses for the use of health-care resources) or especially indirect (sick leaves or reduced performances), as well as very high intangible costs (disruption of family lives and relationships in general, social roles and career opportunities, individual well being).
More than 90% of patients who present to their primary care provider for evaluation of headaches have a primary headache disorder.
Approximately 1 billion dollars each year are spent on unnecessary brain imaging of primary headache disorders.
See differential diagnosis for causes of headache from the International Classification of Headache Disorders 3rd edition.

In a study of 265 patients presenting to a family physician with new onset headache, the following causes were seen: Muscle contraction or tension headache 48%, migraine 30%, cluster headache 2%, post-traumatic headache 6%, drug or OCP induced headache 5%, cervical spine headache 2%, and 1% or less with temporal arteritis, ocular headache, meningitis, rhinitis, wine intolerance, intracranial lesion, demyelinating disorder, or vascular abnormality.

Migraine and tension-type headache can be mistaken for sinus headache or headache attributed to acute rhinosinusitis because of the similarity on location of the headache and, in the case of migraine, because of the commonly accompanying nasal autonomic symptoms (facial pain, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea). The presence or absence of purulent nasal discharge and/or other diagnostic features of acute rhinosinusitis can help to differentiate these conditions. In addition, an episode of migraine can be triggered or exacerbated by nasal or sinus pathology.
Consider red flag symptoms for serious headaches.
For additional information see chapters on migraine, cluster headache, and tension-type headache.

Migraine: The trigeminal nucleus activates meningeal and blood vessel nociceptors and triggers reflex connections with cranial parasympathetics, resulting in vasodilation via vasoactive intestinal polypeptide release.Neuropeptides such as calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide (PACAP) are also gathering evidence as important mediators of migraines. Hypothalamic activation followed by alterations in the thalamo-cortical circuits and cortical spreading with depolarisation contribute to the development of migraines.

Tension-type headache: Nociceptive inputs from posterior cervical, head, and neck myofascial trigger points and peripheral activation of chemical mediators (bradykinin, serotonin, and substance P) in tender muscles create central sensitization.

Trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias: Have lateralized and prominent cranial autonomic symptoms (CASs) medicated predominately by the trigeminal autonomic (parasympathetic) reflex. This pathway can be triggered by a variety of trigeminal nociceptive triggers.
The diagnosis of primary headache disorders is clinical and based on the diagnostic criteria of the International Headache Society (IDCHD-3rd eddition). See

Specific symptoms that best indicate migraine include nausea, photophobia, phonophobia, unilateral, throbbing or pulsing headache, and headache triggered by chocolate or cheese.Symptoms that best rule out migraine are absence of nausea, photophobia, nonthrobbing/pulsating headache, and no exacerbation by physical activity.
Specific symptoms that best indicate cluster headache include strictly unilateral, restlessness, duration of attacks 15 to 180 min, periods of remission, conjunctival injection, and nasal congestion.
Physical examination is often normal for patients with primary headaches, although on rare occasions patients with cluster headache may present with classic signs and symptoms ().

Secondary sources of headache and serious or life-threatening causes of headache should be promptly evaluated in patients with red flag signs or symptoms (see ). Other concerning symptoms that should prompt additional evaluation include three yellow flag (wakes patient from sleep at night, new onset side-locked headaches, and postural headaches).

A systematic review of 22 studies at overall low risk of bias concluded that the history and physical examination has low accuracy for ruling in or ruling out spontaneous subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). The best things to rule in SAH were a focal neurologic deficit (LR+ 4.4), complaint of a stiff neck (LR+ 6.6), and neck stiffness on exam (LR+ 7.3), whereas headache that took more than an hour to develop helped rule out SAH (LR− 0.06).
The best predictors of finding a significant intracranial abnormality on neuroimaging were cluster type headache (LR+ 11) and abnormal neurologic findings on exam (LR+ 5.3).

Thunderclap headache TCH, a high intensity headache reaching maximum intensity in <1min, can be the only initial symptom of SAH. A high sensitivity for SAH can be achieved with a combination of TCH and age older than 40 years, neck pain or stiffness, loss of consciousness, onset during exertion, or limited neck flexion on examination. Keep in mind that TCH also occurs in other neurologic conditions.

A study of 10 years of health records at an academic medical center identified 932 adults presenting to the ED with thunderclap headache. Of these, 393 (42.1%) had aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage; some of these patients were referred from outside institutions. Of the remaining 539 adults, the authors report that 275 (51%) had serious findings: 97 (35.2%) had reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome; 68 (24.7%) had nonaneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage; 27 (9.8%) had nontraumatic intracerebral hemorrhage; 22 (8.0%) had cerebral ischemia; and the rest had brain tumors, encephalopathy, meningitis, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, or neurosurgical complications.
Suspect giant cell arteritis in patients who 50 years or older and present with new onset headache accompanied by visual changes, jaw claudication, or temporal artery symptoms.
Suspect idiopathic intracranial hypertension in female patients of child bearing age that present with headaches, pulsatile tinnitus, and transient vision changes.
Suspect obstructive sleep apnea syndrome in patients that are obese and complaining of morning headaches.
Secondary headache can also be related to substance withdrawal, for instance due to caffeine, opioid and estrogen.

The Erwin Test for Cluster Headache has a sensitivity of 85% and specificity of 89% for cluster headache when yes is answered to all three questions and can therefore aid in reducing diagnostic delay (see Figure 4).

Secondary headache during pregnancy and puerperium has high risk of severe pathology especially if there is an absence of headache history, occurring during the third trimester, or accompanied by seizures, hypertension and fever.
Consider eclampsia in pregnant patients with headache.
ACOG guidelines recommend limiting use of gadolinium if MRI is required. 52
Diagnosis is primarily based on the history and physical examination (see ).

Neuroimaging is indicated in patients with specific symptoms ("red flags") on history or physical examination ().These include focal findings on neurologic examination, thunderclap headache, new onset headache after age 50, malignancy or HIV disease, seizures, or headache precipitated by Valsalva.B

New-onset headache in high-risk populations (eg, known cancer patients) are more likely to have positive findings on CT or MRI. For example, up to 82% of HIV-positive patients have positive intracranial pathology. Similarly, up to 47% of patients presenting with thunderclap headache have a subarachnoid hemorrhage on CT.

Sudden, severe, unilateral headache in a young patient, radiating to the neck and accompanied by ipsilateral Horner's syndrome, is suspicious for carotid or vertebral artery dissection. In a series of 161 patients, 47% with carotid dissection, and 33% with vertebral, reported headache as the initial manifestation. MRI, MRA, CTA, and/or catheter angiography are indicated to identify the lesion.
Both MRI and CT have been shown to be effective imaging modalities in patients with secondary causes of headache.
Neuroimaging is often not necessary in younger patients with symptoms of migraine or tension-type headache.
Lumbar puncture is indicated if there is concern for meningitis.
If SAH is suspected, recent guidelines strongly recommend, based on mid-level evidence, that a nondiagnostic head CT be followed by lumbar puncture.

If subarachnoid hemorrhage is being considered, a CT is most useful to rule out this diagnosis if done in the first 12 to 24 hours after the onset of the headache. A lumbar puncture may not be necessary in patients with low pre-test probability and a negative CT in the first 12 to 24 hours.
In patients presenting with thunderclap headache and a normal neurological examination, a negative brain CT scan within 6 hours of headache onset is highly sensitive in ruling out aneurysmal SAH.
The American Academy of Neurology's "Choosing Wisely" recommendations include not ordering an EEG for patients with headache.
For diagnosing Giant Cell arteritis (GCA), color duplex sonography (CDS) provides high positive predictive value and allows for a significant reduction in temporal artery biopsies.

The 3-item ID Migraine Screener (see ) or click here for interactive rule is a simple, self-administered screening tool that is scored positive if the patient endorses 2 out of 3 variables: nausea, photophobia, and headache-related disability any day in the past 3 months. In a primary care setting, migraine is a highly prevalent and disabling illness that remains substantially underdiagnosed. This screening test has a positive predictive value of 93.3% because of a very good sensitivity of 81% and a specificity of 75%. Thus, is a valid and reliable screening instrument for the primary care setting.
The POUND mnemonic (P: pulsatile, O: hours duration 4-72hr, U: Unilateral, N: Nauseating, D: Disabling) is a useful screen for migraine that uses 5 specific clinical characteristics (see ).

Worrisome features should be part of every headache evaluation and using the SNNOOP10 mnemonic can help identify them. S: Systemic symptoms (fever); N: Neoplasm history; N: Neurologic symptoms/signs (altered consciousness, focal deficits); O: Onset, sudden or abrupt; O: Older age, onset of headache after 50 years; P: Pattern change or recent onset of headache; P: Positional headache; P: Precipitated by sneezing, coughing, or exercise; P: Papilledema; P: Progressive headache and atypical presentations; P: Pregnancy and puerperium; P: Painful eye with autonomic features; P: Posttraumatic onset of headache; P: Pathology of the immune system such as HIV; P: Painkiller overuse or new drug at onset of headache.
The Ottawa Subarachnoid Hemorrhage rule is sensitive for identifying subarachnoid hemorrhage in otherwise alert and neurologically intact patients.

See for a suggested approach to evaluation. Early detection and management of modifiable risk factors, such as migraine progression, medication overuse, obesity, depression, and stressful life events, are also improtant to avoid the chronification of migraine.

tr.td: Migraine Without AuraA. At least five attacks fulfilling criteria B-DB. Headache attacks lasting 4-72 hours (untreated or unsuccesfully treated)C. Headache has at least two of the following four characteristics: Unilateral location Pulsating quality Moderate or severe pain intensity Aggravation by or causing avoidance of routine physical activity (eg, walking or climbing stairs) D. During headache at least one of the following: Nausea and/or vomiting Photophobia and phonophobia E. Not better accounted for by another diagnosis

Migraine With AuraA. At least two attacks fulfilling criteria B and CB. One or more of the following fully reversible aura symptoms: Visual Sensory Speech and/or language Motor Brainstem (eg, vertigo, tinnitus, diplopia, ataxia) Retinal C. At least two of the following six characterisitcs: At least one aura symptom spreads gradually over ≥ 5 minutes Two or more aura symptoms occur in succession Each individual aura symptom lasts 5-60 minutes At least one aura symptom is unilateral At least one aura symptom is positive (scintillations and pins and needles) The aura is accompanied, or followed within 60 minutes, by headache D. Not better accounted for by another diagnosis, and transient ischaemic attack has been excluded

Infrequent Episodic Tension-type Headache A. At least 10 episodes of headache occurring on <1 day per month on average (<12 days per year) and fulﬁlling criteria B-DB. Lasting from 30 minutes to 7 daysC. At least two of the following four characteristics: Bilateral location Pressing or tightening (non-pulsating) quality Mild or moderate intensity Not aggravated by routine physical activity such as walking or climbing stairs D. Both of the following: No nausea or vomiting No more than one of photophobia or phonophobia E. Not better accounted for by another diagnosis.

Chronic Tension-type HeadacheA. Headache occurring on ≥15 days per month on average for >3 months, fulfilling criteria B-DB. Lasting hours to days, or unremittingC. At least 2 of the following: Pressing/tightening (not pulsating) Intensity may inhibit but not prevent daily activities (mild to moderte) Bilateral Not aggravated by routine physical activity D. Both of the following: No more than one of photophobia, phonophobia or mild nausea Neither moderate or severe nausea nor vomiting E. Not better accounted for by another diagnosis

Cluster HeadacheA. At least five attacks fulfilling criteria B-DB. Severe or very severe unilateral orbital, supraorbital and/or temporal pain lasting 15-180 min (when untreated)C. Either or both of the following: 1. At least one of the following symptoms or signs, ipsilaterally to the headache: Conjunctival injection and/or lacrimation nasal congestion and/or rhinorrhea eyelid edema forehead and facial sweating miosis and/or ptosis 2. Sense of restlessness or agitationD. Occuring with a frequency between one every other day and 8 per day for more than half of the time when the disorder is active E. figure.caption: Ottawa SAH Rule
figure.caption_detail: Used in alert patients >15 yr of age with new acute severe nontraumatic headache that reaches maximum intensity within 1 h of onset. Not to be used in patients with new neurological deficits, previous aneurysms, SAH or brain tumors, or a history of similar headaches (≥3 episodes over ≥6 mo).

figure.caption: Three Item Migraine Screener
